interview.question: When you say a family has “kept their home,” how long after rental assistance ends do you mean, and what would you use to confirm the family is still housed?
interview.answer: We enter everything required into the regional homeless data system: enrollments, exits to permanent housing, and how long families were homeless. Case managers log home visits. Honestly we rarely look at our own data beyond the required reports. The board keeps asking whether families are still housed a year after the rent help ends, and whether case management matters beyond the money. We do not have a good answer.

interview.question: During case management, what changes do you hope families make that help them stay housed, and what could staff realistically notice or record during visits?
interview.answer: In the first months families move in fast, usually within 45 days of enrolling, and kids get back into one school. Parents get calmer and start planning instead of reacting. They learn to budget around rent and know who to call when something goes wrong. A year out, what we hope for is that they are still housed, have not gone back to shelter, and have steadier income. Many parents tell us the biggest change is feeling in control again.

interview.question: What does case management look like in practice—what support do families receive, how often do you meet or visit, and for how long?
interview.answer: We serve families with children who are living in shelter or doubled up, referred through the regional coordinated entry system. Most heads of household are single mothers in their twenties and thirties with one to three young kids. Many lost housing after an eviction, a job loss, or leaving a violent relationship. About a third speak Spanish at home. We serve roughly 70 families a year, about 220 people.

interview.question: What kinds of support do case managers typically provide to a family, and how often and for how long do they meet or visit?
interview.answer: Three things. First, rapid rehousing: our housing locator finds an apartment, we pay the security deposit and first month, then step rent help down over up to 12 months. Second, Stay Housed case management: weekly home visits for six months, then monthly, covering budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care and school enrollment. Third, Fresh Start Furniture: volunteers furnish the apartment before move-in day so families walk into a real home.

interview.question: Which grants or contracts fund these services, and what outcomes or reports do those funders ask you to provide?
interview.answer: About 55% of our money is federal homelessness funding passed through the regional Continuum of Care, 20% is state housing funds, 15% comes from local foundations and 10% from individual and congregational donors. The federal and state funders want exits to permanent housing and returns to homelessness. Foundations increasingly ask about family well-being and stories, not just placements.

approved_logic_model.program_name: Keystone Family Housing: Rapid Rehousing, Stay Housed, and Fresh Start Furniture
approved_logic_model.theory_of_change: If Keystone helps families move quickly into permanent housing with time-limited rent assistance, move-in essentials, and voluntary, individualized case management, then families can settle into housing and address barriers that threaten stability. This support is intended to help families remain housed after assistance ends, though housing stability also depends on factors outside Keystone’s control.
inputs: Executive director, four case managers, housing locator, and part-time finance manager
Rental assistance and program operating funds
Small office and regional homeless response system
activities: Identify apartments and help families move into permanent housing
Pay security deposits and first month’s rent, then step down rent help for up to 12 months
Offer voluntary, individualized Stay Housed case management through home visits; frequency is adjusted with each family, with more frequent visits early when appropriate
Help families address budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care, and school enrollment based on their priorities
Provide Fresh Start Furniture move-in support by furnishing apartments before move-in
outputs: Families moved into permanent housing and days from enrollment to move-in
Rental assistance payments and duration of assistance
short_term_outcomes: Families move from homelessness into permanent housing
Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue
Parents report feeling more in control and less stressed
Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected
long_term_outcomes: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends
Fewer families return to homelessness or shelter
assumptions: Families can access suitable, affordable apartments in the local housing market
Families can choose whether to engage in case management and identify supports that fit their needs
Rent assistance, practical move-in support, and case management can address different barriers to housing stability
external_factors: Availability and affordability of rental housing
Changes in household income, employment, and benefit access
Availability of child care, school supports, and other community resources

approved_plan.summary: This plan pairs existing program/HMIS records with a brief, voluntary participant check-in to track housing move-in, families’ confidence, stress, and resource knowledge. It also checks families’ housing status 12 months after move-in, where follow-up is feasible; results are reported as outcomes Keystone contributes to, not outcomes it alone causes. The participant survey has four recommended questions, below the requested limit of about eight.

metrics.name: Permanent-housing move-in and time to move-in
metrics.outcome: Families move from homelessness into permanent housing

questions.text: How many families in the reporting cohort have had the full, comparable observation period to move into housing?
questions.note: Use a consistent cohort definition and observation window, set to match applicable HMIS and award rules; show families not yet observed for the full period separately.

questions.text: How many families in that cohort moved into permanent housing during the observation period?
questions.note: Use the applicable HMIS/award definition for permanent-housing destination and move-in date.

questions.text: Among families who moved in, what was the median number of days from enrollment to move-in?
questions.note: Calculate from enrollment and physical move-in dates for the same cohort and observation period.

metrics.timing: Update enrollment and move-in records as they occur; review by reporting period using a consistent cohort and observation window. Separately show households not yet observed for the full window.
metrics.how_scored: Report the count and share of families in the fully observed cohort who moved into permanent housing, plus median days from enrollment to move-in among those who moved in. Show the cohort size and the not-yet-fully-observed count; align definitions with applicable HMIS and award rules.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families are moving from homelessness into permanent housing and how quickly, a central rapid rehousing result.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC materials frame exits to permanent housing and time homeless as system performance indicators; Connecticut RRH describes helping households move into housing. These are useful alignment points, not automatically the project's required calculation. Confirm award-specific definitions. [S2, S17, S18, S19]

metrics.name: Confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue
metrics.outcome: Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue

questions.text: Think about this same situation each time: you have a problem paying rent or with your landlord. How confident are you that you can take one next step to address it?
questions.note: Ask everyone about the same hypothetical situation at both survey points, whether or not they have a current issue. 0 = not at all confident; 10 = completely confident. Locally adapted check-in, not the validated housing self-efficacy scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you would know what to do if your landlord did not respond to a concern?
questions.note: Optional alternative; use the same hypothetical situation and 0–10 anchors at both survey points. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you could find someone or an organization to help with a rent or landlord issue?
questions.note: Optional alternative; overlaps somewhat with the separate resource-knowledge item. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at a consistent later point, such as program exit or the end of case-management support. Ask the same hypothetical scenario and item both times, after urgent intake needs are addressed.
metrics.how_scored: Report the item’s score distribution and median change for participants with paired answers, alongside baseline, follow-up, paired-response, and missing counts. Do not use a 1-point improvement threshold as a validated measure of meaningful change.
metrics.why_it_matters: A change in confidence can show whether families feel more able to take a next step when a housing problem arises.
metrics.funder_relevance: Housing-specific self-efficacy has been studied with people who are homeless or vulnerably housed. This brief locally adapted question adds a family-level view of a support outcome; it does not replace housing-status reporting. [S20]

metrics.name: Parent-reported stress
metrics.outcome: Parents report feeling more in control and less stressed

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel that problems were too much to handle?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Response options: Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Very often. Do not combine a subset into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel worried about things you could not control?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Use the same five response options; do not combine items into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel you had enough support to manage your worries?
questions.note: Optional locally written item; higher frequency may indicate more support, not necessarily less stress. Do not combine it with the other items as a validated score.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items; use the same past-month time frame and response choices.
metrics.how_scored: Report responses to each item separately, with paired-response and missing counts. Lower frequency on the two included stress items suggests improvement. These are locally written items, not a validated scale; do not calculate a PSS-10 score. Confirm permission terms before reproducing or adapting any PSS-10 wording.
metrics.why_it_matters: Offers a brief view of parents’ reported stress while families work through housing-related challenges.
metrics.funder_relevance: The Community Foundation for Greater New Haven describes dignity and well-being as relevant to basic-needs work; this is a supplementary family-well-being measure, not a stated required metric. The PSS references inform the stress topic only; these items are not PSS-10 items. [S8, S21, S22]

metrics.name: Knowing where to seek help for a chosen need
metrics.outcome: Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know who you could contact?
questions.note: Offer Yes or No; participants may skip instead of answering. Keep the need broad and do not record personal details. At each survey point, record only its broad category where possible.

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know one place you could go for help?
questions.note: Optional alternative with the same broad-need and privacy guidance; locally adapted, not a validated test.

questions.text: Would you like help finding someone to contact about the need you chose?
questions.note: Optional service-planning alternative, not itself a measure of the outcome.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items. Compare answers over time only when the same broad need category is being discussed; if it changed or is unknown, report the answers separately rather than as a direct change.
metrics.how_scored: Report Yes, No, skipped, and missing responses separately. For paired comparisons, include only participants whose broad need category stayed the same. Record whether resource information was offered or accessed only if this can be done without personal details.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether parents feel they know where to turn for help with a priority they chose, consistent with individualized case management.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD housing-search and case-management resources include assessment and mainstream-resource referral tools, and 211 Connecticut provides housing and human-service referral information. This is a practical local check, not a stated funder requirement. [S23, S24]

metrics.name: Housing status 12 months after move-in
metrics.outcome: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends

questions.text: How many families are due for a 12-month housing-status follow-up after move-in?
questions.note: Set each family’s follow-up due date from the recorded physical move-in date. Use a consistent follow-up window. A 6-month check may also be collected where feasible, but the 12-month check is the priority.

questions.text: How many families due for follow-up were contacted, and how many had a known housing status?
questions.note: Keep contacted and known-status counts separate in the record. Use a consent-based, preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts; no impact on services. HMIS may not capture homelessness outside its system.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in permanent housing at follow-up?
questions.note: Count a move to another permanent unit as permanent housing; use consistent definitions at each follow-up window.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were staying in shelter, outside, or another place not meant for housing?
questions.note: Record the status source and follow-up date. Self-report supplements but is not equivalent to HUD’s HMIS-based system return-to-homelessness measure.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in another or unstable housing situation?
questions.note: Use a consistent local status definition; keep this category separate from permanent housing, homelessness, and unknown status.

metrics.timing: Prioritize a follow-up 12 months after each family’s recorded physical move-in date; collect a 6-month status after move-in too only where feasible. Use HMIS or a consent-based, brief follow-up with the family’s preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts. Do not imply every family can be reached.
metrics.how_scored: For each follow-up window, report the number due, contacted, with known status, and with unknown status. Among families with known status, report permanent housing, homelessness, and other/unstable housing separately; include the numerator and denominator for the share housed. Also show the number in permanent housing out of all families due, clearly labeled as including unknowns in the denominator. Unknown status is not evidence of either retention or housing loss. Treat any self-reported return as supplementary to, not equivalent to, the HMIS-based system measure; this is a contribution measure, not proof of program-caused retention.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families are in permanent housing 12 months after move-in while making follow-up coverage and unknown status visible. This is a useful check on housing stability, though it may not always fall after rental assistance ends.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC system performance materials track permanent-housing exits and returns to homelessness; Connecticut RRH guidance provides the program context. A local 12-month follow-up from move-in is a practical measure, not an asserted state requirement, and self-report does not replace HMIS system reporting. [S6, S18, S25, S26]

tools.name: Brief participant check-in
tools.when: Offer at entry and at a consistent later point, after urgent intake needs are addressed. Use a short script: taking part is voluntary, any question may be skipped, and answers will not affect services. Offer read-aloud and translated options where available; use the same wording and response choices each time. The four included questions cover confidence, stress, and resource knowledge; optional items remain off unless Keystone chooses to add them.
metrics: Confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue
Knowing where to seek help for a chosen need

tools.name: Housing outcomes and follow-up records
tools.when: Use program records/HMIS throughout enrollment and move-in, with consistent cohort definitions and observation windows. Prioritize 12-month status after physical move-in; use a consent-based preferred contact method, limited attempts, and report due, contacted, known, and unknown status separately.
metrics: Permanent-housing move-in and time to move-in
